messages.author: c8e6cf811df8eba2
messages.subject: plot.pls
parts:
Hi everyone,

I'm trying to create plots using plot.pls function but although I use the latest version of geomorph (4.0.5), I can't use plot.pls (as well as plot.procd.lm). I also tried 4.0.1 version and tried to update all dependent packages and re-installed the package several times.

I actually want to visualize the magnitude and direction of variables on the shape using biplots.

Also I'd like to see explained variation by the PLS axes but created object and summary function don't provide such an information. Am I doing something wrong?

Thanks,
Fatih.

messages.author: fbfd20ce829c6c6c
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] plot.pls
parts:
Hi Faith, 

Since you did not provide code, I'm wondering if you could confirm that you're using something like 

Mod <- procD.lm(...)
plot(Mod)

and not 

plot.procD.lm(Mod).

The former is the correct usage of functions like plot or summary, as applied to specific kinds of objects. This may be the issue?

Best,
Bryan

messages.author: fbfd20ce829c6c6c
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] plot.pls
parts:
If pls <- two.b.pls(malesym.gdf$Coords, malevariables), 
then plot(pls) or summary(pls) is what you want. 

PLS does not output % variance of the original variables. You could obtain this yourself by regressing the data onto the PLS scores (e.g., pls$left.pls.vectors, $right.pls.vectors) with procD.pgls. It also looks like you might have many variables measured for the males. It might make more sense to use procD.pgls, which would let you test specific hypotheses for each variable, instead of treating them as a whole and using two.b.pls. 

Creating a biplot for the shape data is non-sensical, I think. This is because landmarks should not be interpreted individually and therefore knowing which landmarks relate to a PCA of the shape data is not informative. Biplots are typically used to visualize variable loadings on a rotation of the original data (like loadings on PCA or MDS axes) – PCA and MDS axes are independent axes of variation in a single dataset. This is distinct from PLS axes which are axes representing the directions through two multivariate datasets which maximize the covariance between them. This is just my intuition and I am happy to update my understanding if others have any ideas.

Bryan
